title: Visitor and Harvest
premise: Juniper Vasquez, a nonbinary property surveyor who has spent three years renting the cheapest room in a house that hums, creaks, and occasionally answers, is hired to appraise the property before its demolition. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside—sealed by someone who knew what was coming—the house's long-tolerated noises stop being deniable, and Juniper learns the previous tenants didn't leave; they were harvested, one invitation at a time. As night falls and the crew vanishes room by room, Juniper discovers their own three years of quiet survival were never invisibility but a slow courtship: the house has been deciding whether to keep them or spend them. In the climax, Juniper offers the one thing the house cannot take—a freely given goodbye rather than a stolen soul—and walks out at sunrise as the structure finally exhales, leaving behind a door now sealed from the outside.
about_author: Mara Almeida is a former building inspector from coastal Rhode Island who spent a decade writing reports about houses no one should live in. Her fiction transforms the bureaucratic language of property into something that breathes.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. Arriving to conduct the final pre-demolition appraisal, Juniper catalogs the house's defects with practiced detachment while noting small wrongnesses: rooms measured differently on return visits, a draft that follows him. The emotional beat is brittle professionalism masking dread he refuses to name.

chapters.title: Three Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: POV Juniper, flashback woven through the inspection day. We learn how Juniper came to rent here after losing everything, and how each noise got a rational explanation—pipes, settling, raccoons. The beat is the comfort and cost of self-deception; belonging bought with willful blindness.

chapters.title: Crew Day
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. The excavation crew arrives early, loud and cheerful, breaking the house's long silence. Juniper feels oddly protective of the walls even as machinery tears at the yard. The beat is guilt—he invited these people into something he half-understands.

chapters.title: What the Backhoe Found
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. Beneath the foundation, the crew uncovers a heavy door, its hinges rusted shut, sealed from the inside with iron and salt and something like fingernail marks. The foreman jokes; the youngest worker goes pale. The beat is the collapse of every explanation Juniper built.

chapters.title: Inventory of Absences
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. Researching the property records, Juniper finds gaps: tenants listed, then struck through, census pages torn. Every seven years, someone new signs the lease. The beat is cold clarity—Juniper's cheap rent was never luck.

chapters.title: The House Stops Pretending
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. At dusk the crew packs up for the day; the house's ambient sounds cease entirely, and the silence is worse. Doors stand open that were always locked. The beat is exposure—the invisibility Juniper cultivated is revoked.

chapters.title: Dana
chapters.summary: POV Dana, the young crew member who stayed late to photograph the door. She hears her own voice calling from inside the house when she knows she's outside it. The beat is the first harvest beginning, seen from the victim's side, disorientation curdling into terror.

chapters.title: Headcount
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. The foreman calls roll; Dana doesn't answer. Her truck is still there, engine warm, phone ringing inside the walls. The others want to call police; the phones show full bars and connect to nothing. The beat is dawning collective horror and Juniper's shame surfacing.

chapters.title: Rules of the Lease
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. Searching the attic, Juniper finds his original lease annotated in handwriting matching his own—clauses he never read: occupancy constitutes consent; departure requires notice; notice requires sunrise. The beat is terrible recognition that he signed himself over without reading.

chapters.title: The Previous Tenants
chapters.summary: POV Juniper, intercut with fragments of past tenants' voices in the walls. He finds their belongings curated like exhibits: glasses, a child's shoe, a wedding ring, all arranged facing the sealed door. The beat is grief—the house keeps trophies, and it has already started a shelf for him.

chapters.title: Bargaining
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. He tries to negotiate aloud, offering money, offering to stay longer, offering anything but himself. The house responds by showing him warmth: his childhood kitchen, his mother's voice, everything he lost rendered perfectly. The beat is temptation—the price of survival suddenly looks affordable.

chapters.title: Marcus Runs
chapters.summary: POV Marcus, the foreman, who decides the whole thing is a prank and bolts for the gate. The yard extends; the road recedes; he ends up back at the front door without ever turning around. The beat is futility—the property line is not where the maps say.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. Through the sealed door's keyhole, Juniper sees the thing beneath the house: vast, patient, wearing the faces of everyone it has taken, including, briefly, his own. It was invited once, long ago, by the first owner—and invitations can be amended. The beat is awe and revulsion entwined.

chapters.title: The Long Night Begins
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. Clocks in the house run backward; midnight approaches and un-approaches. Juniper barricades the kitchen with salt from the excavation site and realizes the salt only works where he truly believes he belongs. The beat is the theme made mechanical: survival depends on claiming a place.

chapters.title: Voices in His Voice
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. The house speaks in Juniper's own voice, arguing both sides of his head: stay and be safe forever, or walk out and lose everything again. He nearly answers yes. The beat is identity under siege—the horror isn't being eaten but being edited.

chapters.title: Dana, Still
chapters.summary: POV Dana, existing somewhere between rooms. She finds the other taken ones, dim and placid, and refuses to become furniture. She scratches a message toward the living world: IT ONLY KEEPS WHAT SURRENDERS. The beat is resistance kindling in the harvested.

chapters.title: Amendment
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. Remembering the lease clause about notice, Juniper understands the loophole: consent can be withdrawn in writing before sunrise, witnessed by another tenant. But the other tenants are dead—or are they? He hears Dana's scratching. The beat is desperate hope with a deadline attached.

chapters.title: The House Offers Everything
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. The final temptation: the house shows him a life where he was never evicted, never broke, never alone—himself, belonging, effortless. All he must do is stop resisting. He weeps, and almost stays. The beat is the darkest hour; the price of survival looks like peace.

chapters.title: Witness
chapters.summary: POV Juniper and Dana alternating. Juniper breaks through to the between-space where Dana holds on, and they write the amendment together—her hand guiding his, two signatures, one withdrawal of consent. The house screams in every voice it owns. The beat is solidarity as weapon; belonging chosen, not granted.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. Carrying Dana's fading form toward the door, Juniper endures the house's last assault—it becomes every place he ever belonged and every place that rejected him. The sky lightens. The lease burns in his hands. The beat is endurance rewarded at the exact cost of everything false.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Outside
chapters.summary: POV Juniper. On the lawn at dawn, Juniper watches the house settle into true, ordinary silence. Crew members wake in their trucks remembering nothing. Using the excavator, Juniper seals the unearthed door from the outside—not trapping anything, but ending the invitation. The beat is exhausted agency; some survivals look like demolition.

chapters.title: Notice Given
chapters.summary: POV Juniper, weeks later. He files the appraisal honestly: structure condemned, do not occupy. Renting a bright apartment he chose himself, he still checks the walls at night—but now he listens without explaining. The beat is resolution with scars: belonging is not a place you're given, but a claim you keep making.
